title: The Atlantic’s “Unthinkable” Project Ranked 50 Trump-Era Incidents
description_short: The Atlantic catalogued 50 incidents from Trump’s first term, ranking them subjectively by outlandishness and importance.
description_medium: The Atlantic described its “Unthinkable” project as a catalog of 50 incidents from the midpoint of Trump’s first term, ranked subjectively for outlandishness and importance. A linked explainer was published January 14, 2019. The available material supports the magazine’s editorial project and framing, not a measured democratic-stability effect or a continuing risk signal in March 2026.
description_long: The Atlantic’s landing page introduces “Donald Trump’s 50 Most Unthinkable Moments” as a review of 50 incidents from the first Trump presidency. The magazine says it chose incidents it considered improbable, norm-bending, and destructive, and explicitly describes its ranking as highly subjective, based on outlandishness and importance. A linked video explainer featuring editor in chief Jeffrey Goldberg was published January 14, 2019, and explains the project as an attempt to chronicle bizarre and dangerous moments of the presidency. These sources document an editorial catalog and the publication’s own description of its selection. They do not show that the magazine measured democratic stability, identified a mitigation plan, or continued to issue a specific risk signal in March 2026. The frozen record’s March 4, 2026 date and continuing-risk wording are not retained because the accessible evidence connects the project to the 2019 midterm of Trump’s first term. January 14 is the linked explainer’s publication date and earliest archive capture date for the landing page; the landing page’s original release timestamp remains uncertain. This entry describes editorial coverage, not an independent finding of harm.
date_precision: The Atlantic explainer and earliest accessible archived landing page are dated January 14, 2019; the original landing-page release timestamp is not exposed.

title: Unverified Allegation That Kash Patel Ordered Journalist Arrests
description_short: The supplied record alleges journalist arrests under Patel; no matching arrest or charge is substantiated in the packet.
description_medium: The supplied record alleges that FBI Director Kash Patel ordered investigative journalists arrested and charged under the Espionage Act in August 2025 over leaked government material. The prior packet says it found no matching credible report or official record, and supplies no names, charging documents, or source URLs. This draft preserves the allegation only as unverified internal copy; it does not state that arrests or charges occurred.
description_long: An earlier Trump Files record alleges that, in August 2025, FBI Director Kash Patel ordered the arrest of several journalists who were investigating administration corruption. It further alleges that they were charged under the Espionage Act for possessing leaked government documents and that press-freedom groups condemned the arrests. These are claims carried forward from the supplied synopsis, not independently established facts. The supplied research note says it did not find credible reporting or an official record matching the alleged arrests, charges, and date. No journalist is named, and the packet contains no arrest record, indictment, FBI or Justice Department statement, source URL, or attributable press-freedom organization comment. The supplied August 7 date is also unverified. This internal draft should not be read as evidence that any journalist was arrested or charged; it records only the allegation and the exact missing support. Publication eligibility is false unless a primary record or reliable contemporaneous report establishes the event, identities, charges, date, and source of the criticism.

description_long: The supplied review packet identifies a narrower candidate event than the frozen title: it says the Pentagon issued Hegseth’s “Restoring America’s Fighting Force” guidance on January 29, 2025, directing department-wide elimination of DEI offices and initiatives. That date corrects the original January 25 label only if the guidance itself is the event; the packet does not include a memorandum or cite a source URL. It also does not verify the frozen record’s claims that diversity officers were fired on Hegseth’s first day, that all DEI training had already been removed across DoD, or that the policy harmed readiness or drove service members out. Those are not treated as established outcomes here. This internal copy preserves only the supplied policy proposition and keeps the officer-firing and readiness claims marked unverified. title: DHS Ends Afghanistan’s TPS Designation Effective July 14, 2025
description_short: DHS terminated Afghanistan’s Temporary Protected Status designation, effective July 14, 2025.
description_medium: On May 13, 2025, DHS published a notice terminating Afghanistan’s Temporary Protected Status designation, effective July 14. The notice estimates about 11,700 Afghan nationals and people without nationality last resident in Afghanistan held TPS; it separately notes about 3,600 were also approved lawful permanent residents. The sourced action concerns Afghanistan only and does not establish deportations or simultaneous TPS terminations for other nationalities.
description_long: On May 13, 2025, DHS published a notice terminating Afghanistan’s designation for Temporary Protected Status (TPS). The notice says the Secretary reviewed country conditions, consulted other U.S. agencies, and determined that Afghanistan no longer met the statutory conditions for TPS. The designation ended effective at 11:59 p.m. local time on July 14, 2025. DHS estimated approximately 11,700 Afghan nationals and people without nationality who last habitually resided in Afghanistan held TPS under that designation. The notice also states that approximately 3,600 of that group had already been approved as lawful permanent residents. This entry is narrowed to the Afghanistan designation; it does not claim that Ukraine, Venezuela, Haiti, El Salvador, or other designations ended in the same March action. The notice establishes a change in legal status, not that former TPS holders were deported, returned to danger, or all lacked another immigration status. Those individual outcomes and the legal merits of the Secretary’s assessment are outside the evidence used here.
